findings.title: PowerShell.exe opened LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, SourceProcessGUID {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1F3FFF within the same second. This is the access mask required to read LSASS memory for credential dumping and is not normal for PowerShell. It occurs in the same session/user context (pbeesly) that ran the Invoke-Exfil PowerShell script on this host, indicating an adversary dumping credentials.

findings.title: LSASS wrote SAM account data on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:10, lsass.exe (PID 748) set the registry value HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F. This is the SAM account database key. The write is performed by lsass.exe itself (the legitimate owner of the SAM hive), so it is consistent with normal OS behavior rather than an external dumping tool; no reg save / hive-copy activity was observed. Recorded as suspicious context only.

findings.title: LSASS updated cached domain credential store (HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1)
findings.summary: lsass.exe repeatedly set HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 on nashua.dmevals.local (03:11:40, 03:12:46, 03:13:49, 03:15:03) and on scranton.dmevals.local (03:20:46). The SECURITY\Cache\NL$ keys are the cached domain credential store, but the writes are made by lsass.exe itself, which legitimately maintains this cache during logon. No external process read or copied the hive, so this reflects normal OS credential-cache maintenance rather than dumping.

The only packet-capture activity in the dataset is the legitimate Azure Network Watcher agent. On scranton.dmevals.local, NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (running as SYSTEM, parent services.exe) launched 'netsh.exe trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\...\*.etl"' at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z and 'netsh.exe trace stop' at 03:19:24Z. The agent binary resides under C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\ and was also invoked with /service, Install /service /autoStart, Start /service /autoStart and Test /service /autoStart. This is Azure platform diagnostic capture, not adversary sniffing.

This is the standard Azure Windows Guest Agent diagnostic tracing, not adversary network sniffing.

findings.summary: Hunting for classic network-sniffing artifacts returned nothing: no tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap/dumpcap/tshark/pktmon process executions, no npcap/winpcap/pcap driver image loads (sysmon event 6 = 0 hits), and no promiscuous/raw-socket command lines. The single 'raw' command-line match was a PowerShell steganography loader (System.Drawing bitmap decode + IEX), unrelated to sniffing. Zeek showed only routine weird/notice events (self-signed SSL certs), no ICMP tunneling or sniffing indicators. The PsExec/sdelete64 activity on scranton is lateral movement/anti-forensics, not T1040.

Immediately before, at 03:06:47, the same user defined a 'Keystroke-Check' function that enumerates known antivirus processes (avp, acs, outpost, mcvsescn, mcods, navapsvc, kav, AvastSvc, AvastUi, nod32krn, nod32, ekern, dwengine, MsMpEng, msseces, ekrn, savservice, scfservice, savadminservice) — a hallmark anti-AV check of the Get-Keystrokes keylogger tool. The job was later viewed (03:07:36) and removed (03:07:49). This is a keylogger capturing keystrokes on the host.

findings.title: PowerShell full-access handle to LSASS and private-key/clipboard capture on scranton
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16 UTC on scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, entity {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and then 0x1FFFFF — full process access consistent with reading credential memory. In the same session user pbeesly ran 'Get-PrivateKeys' (dumping certificate private keys to .pfx files using a hardcoded password 'saribas'), 'Get-Clipboard', and 'Invoke-ScreenCapture'. Together these are input/credential capture actions on the host.

findings.title: Invoke-ScreenCapture GUI capture function executed by pbeesly on scranton
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:53 UTC on scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly defined and invoked an 'Invoke-ScreenCapture' function that uses System.Windows.Forms.SystemInformation::VirtualScreen and System.Drawing to repeatedly capture the screen to .bmp files in the user's Downloads folder, then ran 'Invoke-ScreenCapture;Start-Sleep -Seconds 3;View-Job -JobName "Screenshot"'. This is GUI/screen input capture on the host.

findings.title: wsmprovhost.exe remote PowerShell session opened LSASS with full access on nashua
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:09:29 UTC on nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, entity {5aa8ec29-e463-5eac-6303-000000000400}) — the host process for remote PowerShell (WinRM) sessions — opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF. The call trace runs through Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, indicating a PowerShell cmdlet in a remote session requested full access to LSASS memory. This is consistent with credential API access from a remote PowerShell session, though no explicit hooking DLL was observed.

findings.title: No brute-force authentication activity observed; credential access on scranton used LSASS memory access instead
findings.summary: Across windows.security (41002 events, 02:55-03:28Z) there are zero 4625 failed-logon events, so no brute-force authentication pattern exists. The only 'logon/password' hits in windows.other are benign (RDP session logon succeeded for DMEVALS\pbeesly, Customer Experience logon notification, PTR registration failure). The genuine credential-access activity on scranton.dmevals.local is LSASS memory access by PowerShell.exe (GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF) and a Get-PrivateKeys certificate-export script, which are not brute-force techniques.

findings.title: No offline password-cracking artifacts; LSASS handle opens are the credential-access mechanism
findings.summary: No SAM/SECURITY hive reads under 4663/4656/4670 (C112 zero hits; the 'SAM' ObjectName values are benign registry key names). The 326 lsass handle opens (C115) are dominated by svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (benign), but PowerShell.exe opened lsass.exe with 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) on scranton at 03:05:16 — a credential-dumping indicator, not password cracking.

findings.title: No password-spraying activity; 4648 explicit-credential logons are PSEXESVC lateral movement
findings.summary: No 4625 events exist (C118/C119/C121 zero hits), so there is no spray pattern. findings.title: No credential-stuffing activity; no failed logons and no leaked-credential reuse pattern
findings.summary: No 4625 events exist in windows.security (C125/C126/C127 zero hits) and no password-bearing command lines in sysmon (C130 zero hits). The only credential reuse is pbeesly's own valid credentials used via PsExec/4648 for lateral movement, which is not credential stuffing.

findings.title: No MFA interception activity; 'Credential' hits are benign Windows internals
findings.summary: Hunting for T1111 (Multi-Factor Authentication Interception) across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other produced no evidence of MFA/token/smart-card interception. All 'Credential'-related hits are standard Windows components: Wininit event 14 logging 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' (Credential Guard disabled) on scranton, lsass.exe setting HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled to 0x00000000 at boot, and services.exe registering the built-in CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service. Explicit-credential logons (4648) are dominated by user pbeesly via C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe (PsExec) and normal winlogon/svchost/taskhostw processes. LSASS handle access (Sysmon 10) is almost entirely svchost.exe/powershell.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION), consistent with benign security tooling. No MFA provider, OTP, smart-card or token-interception artifacts were observed.

findings.title: WebDAV forced-authentication coercion from scranton (10.0.1.4) to 192.168.0.4
findings.summary: Host 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local) attempted SMB to 192.168.0.4 on ports 445 and 139, all of which were rejected (zeek.conn_state REJ), then immediately fell back to WebDAV over HTTP port 80. The first probe used the 'DavClnt' user agent (OPTIONS / -> 403), followed by a sustained series of 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362' requests (OPTIONS, PROPFIND, PUT, LOCK, HEAD) against /webdav and /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z, many answered 401 Unauthorized before succeeding (PUT 201/204, LOCK 200, HEAD 200, PROPFIND 207). This SMB-reject-then-WebDAV-fallback sequence with the Windows WebDAV redirector user agent is the classic T1187 forced-authentication pattern used to coerce a victim host into authenticating to an attacker-controlled WebDAV/SMB listener and leak NTLM credentials. All 36 WebDAV method requests in the dataset originate solely from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4.

findings.title: Credential-bearing SMB share access from 10.0.1.4 to SYSVOL/IPC$/ADMIN$
findings.summary: The same source 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local) generated network share access events on newyork.dmevals.local and nashua.dmevals.local, reaching \\*\SYSVOL, \\*\IPC$ and \\*\ADMIN$ with access masks such as 0x120089/0x12019f/0x17019f (read/write/execute-style masks) as accounts SCRANTON$ and pbeesly. This is consistent with the credential-bearing SMB activity that accompanies the WebDAV coercion, though SYSVOL/IPC$/ADMIN$ access is also common in legitimate domain administration, so it is assessed as suspicious rather than definitively malicious on its own.

findings.title: PowerShell remoting host (wsmprovhost.exe) opened LSASS with full access on NASHUA during attacker session
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:09:29.430Z, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, the WinRM/PowerShell-remoting host) opened C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff (full access). The call trace runs through PowerShell's Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, i.e. the access was driven by a PowerShell command executed in the remoting session, not by an OS component. This is the only non-system/non-AV process to touch LSASS in the dataset. It occurred seconds after user pbeesly ran 'Invoke-Command -ComputerName NASHUA -ScriptBlock { Get-Process -IncludeUserName ... }' from scranton, and the same pbeesly session on NASHUA then enumerated and archived credential-relevant files (*pass*, *login*, *admin*, *vpn) with Compress-Archive/Rar.exe. This is consistent with exploitation/abuse of the remoting channel to reach credential material in LSASS.

findings.title: Attacker used PsExec with cleartext credentials to reach NASHUA before the LSASS access
findings.summary: From scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly repeatedly launched PsExec64.exe against \\NASHUA supplying the account password in cleartext on the command line ('-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe') at 03:11:18, 03:12:25, 03:13:28 and 03:14:42. This lateral movement to NASHUA precedes the wsmprovhost.exe LSASS access at 03:09:29 and the file-collection/archiving activity on NASHUA, showing the operator already held valid credentials and was operating interactively on the remote host.

findings.title: Routine LSASS handle accesses by system/AV/telemetry processes are benign
findings.summary: The bulk of Sysmon event 10 hits targeting lsass.exe come from legitimate components: svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (query-limited), Microsoft Azure IaaSAntimalware AntimalwareConfig.exe and WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe with 0x1400/0x1000, and wininit.exe/csrss.exe with 0x1fffff at boot. These are normal OS/security-product behaviours and are not exploitation for credential access.

findings.title: WebDAV DavSetCookie process creation is benign WebDAV client cookie handling
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly, rundll32.exe was spawned by svchost.exe with command line 'rundll32.exe C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav' (5 occurrences, 2020-05-01 23:08:50 to 23:10:23). This is the standard Windows WebDAV client (davclnt.dll) setting a WebDAV cookie for the mapped http://192.168.0.4/webdav share, not theft of a browser session cookie. The same command line appears in Sysmon process-creation events on the same host.

findings.title: INetCookies file creation by svchost is a WARP JIT service package artifact
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, svchost.exe (PID 7200, SYSTEM) created C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-b484-4973-bbf2-a04208ecd4d4\AC\INetCookies at 2020-05-02T03:21:05.681Z. This is a per-package WinINet cookie store under the LocalService service profile for the Windows WARP JIT package, created by a system service, not a browser session cookie being stolen. No browser cookie database (Chrome/Edge/Firefox Cookies, Login Data, WebCache) was created or accessed anywhere in the dataset.

findings.title: No browser cookie-store access or cookie-stealing tooling observed
findings.summary: Across windows.sysmon, windows.security, windows.powershell and windows.other, the only 'cookie'-related artifacts are the benign WebDAV DavSetCookie and the WARP JIT INetCookies file. Sysmon process-access (event 10) to browser processes (MicrosoftEdge.exe, MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe, MicrosoftEdgeSH.exe) and lsass.exe came only from svchost.exe and Explorer.EXE with routine access masks (0x1000, 0x2000, 0x3000), consistent with normal system operation rather than memory scraping for session cookies. No PowerShell script block, process command line, or file creation referenced browser cookie databases or cookie-theft utilities.

findings.title: Adjacent credential/exfil activity found but it is not web session cookie theft
findings.summary: While hunting T1539 I observed related attacker activity that is NOT cookie theft: on scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly ran PsExec64.exe with plaintext credentials ('-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by') to execute C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on \\NASHUA, and a PowerShell script block 'Invoke-Exfil' (Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1) that 7-Zips the user's Downloads folder with a password and copies it to a WebDAV share at \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials. sdelete64.exe was then used to delete archives (working.zip, Draft.Zip, SysinternalsSuite.zip). This is credential use and data exfiltration, not theft of web session cookies, so it does not satisfy T1539.

findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys script exported machine certificates to .pfx on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script block (ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) defining function Get-PrivateKeys. It enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and calls Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a Thumbprint, writing each to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas'. The script executed: powershell.exe created C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx at 03:04:57 and the file was later accessed/deleted at 03:08:51. This is direct private-key/certificate theft (T1552.004).

findings.title: accesschk.exe created a file named passwordsDB on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly launched C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\accessChk.exe (PID 9204) at 03:04:34, and one second later the process created the file C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB. The name is credential-themed, but accesschk is a legitimate Sysinternals ACL-inspection tool and the created file sits in its own install directory, consistent with a tool output/log artifact rather than harvested credentials. No credential content was observed in the file. Treated as suspicious-but-unconfirmed for T1552.

findings.title: SMB reads of GptTmpl.inf from Default Domain Policy by machine accounts
findings.summary: Zeek smb_files records show hosts 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 opening \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\sysvol paths including dmevals.local\Policies\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}\Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT\SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf. Windows security 5145 events on newyork.dmevals.local show the same GptTmpl.inf read by machine accounts SCRANTON$ and NASHUA$. This is the standard Default Domain Policy GUID being read during normal Group Policy processing by computer accounts, not GPP cpassword harvesting (no Groups.xml/cpassword access observed).

findings.title: Explicit-credential logons (4648) by pbeesly to NASHUA via PsExec
findings.summary: 15 event.code 4648 explicit-credential logons were observed. pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local used explicit credentials targeting server NASHUA, and on nashua.dmevals.local C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe performed 4648 logons as pbeesly to localhost. The remaining 4648s are routine winlogon/taskhostw DWM/UMFD/machine-account logons. This reflects PsExec-based lateral movement using pbeesly's own credentials, not credentials harvested from files; no file-based credential source was observed.

findings.title: Registry Password/Credential value sets are OS-internal, not credential storage
findings.summary: 17 Sysmon event.code 13 registry value sets matched Password/Credential paths. All are legitimate OS activity: svchost.exe setting HKU\.DEFAULT\Software\Microsoft\IdentityCRL\ProviderPasswordLength/CharacterGroups on nashua and scranton, lsass.exe setting DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled, services.exe registering CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc, and winlogon.exe setting Winlogon\PasswordExpiryNotification. No adversary-written credential values were found.

findings.title: No shell-history credential access observed
findings.summary: No events referencing consolehost_history or PowerShell history files were found in windows.sysmon process-creation or windows.security file-access data. No shell-history credential collection was observed.

On 2020-05-02 between 03:04 and 03:09 UTC, user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran a PowerShell toolkit (loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1 / readme.ps1) that included credential-access functions. At 03:05:16 the PowerShell process opened a handle to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1FFFFF (full access incl. read/write process memory), and Sysmon recorded the same PowerShell.exe->lsass.exe access with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff. The same session defined and invoked Get-PrivateKeys, which enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and exports every certificate with a private key to .pfx files in the user's Downloads folder using the hardcoded password 'saribas'. This is credential/secret theft from the host's password/certificate stores, followed by staging (Invoke-Exfil compressing Downloads to OfficeSupplies.7z and copying to \\192.168.0.4\webdav) and cleanup (Invoke-BeachCleanup deleting *.pfx).

This is the same actor (pbeesly) who minutes earlier on SCRANTON opened LSASS with full access and exported certificate private keys, and who at 03:09:23 ran Invoke-Command -ComputerName NASHUA. Access to LSASS memory is the mechanism used to harvest Windows Credential Manager / DPAPI secrets, though no explicit vault/DPAPI object access was logged.

findings.summary: The majority of LSASS process-access events are routine: svchost.exe, services.exe, csrss.exe, wininit.exe, taskhostw.exe, RuntimeBroker.exe, backgroundTaskHost.exe, dsregcmd.exe, sppsvc.exe, wmiprvse.exe and Windows Defender MsMpEng.exe opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000/0x1400/0x1478/0x1fffff as part of normal OS operation. Also benign is lsass.exe itself opening C:\Windows\Temp\sdelete64.exe (0x1478) — the reverse direction, part of SDelete's normal operation. The WindowsAzure CollectGuestLogs.exe reading lsass.exe (0x1410) on all four hosts is Azure guest-log collection. These are not credential theft.
findings.title: Benign LSASS handle accesses by system processes

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, running as SYSTEM) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1f3fff, the classic handle access used to read credential material from LSASS. The same host/user context (pbeesly) also ran an Invoke-Exfil PowerShell script (03:08:02Z) that compresses data and copies it to a WebDAV share, and performed PsExec-style explicit-credential logons to nashua.dmevals.local. The bulk of LSASS handle events (289 from svchost.exe with 0x1000, plus Azure antimalware/telemetry with 0x1400) are benign system behaviour.

findings.title: Network logons are machine-account/DC replication traffic, no DC authentication backdoor
findings.summary: The 218 LogonType 3 (network) 4624 events are dominated by the machine account NEWYORK$ logging on to newyork.dmevals.local from ::1, fe80:: and 10.0.0.4 — normal computer-account/DC authentication traffic. The 15 explicit-credential 4648 events are pbeesly authenticating to NASHUA via PSEXESVC.exe (lateral movement) and routine winlogon DWM/UMFD localhost logons. No evidence of a domain-controller authentication backdoor (no Skeleton Key / DSRM / authentication-package tampering).

findings.title: No MFA configuration tampering

findings.title: No network provider DLL registered
findings.summary: No 4657 registry change to NetworkProvider/Credential keys (0 hits) and no PowerShell referencing NetworkProvider/New-Item for a provider DLL (0 hits). No rogue network provider DLL was installed to capture credentials.

findings.title: No adversary-in-the-middle activity observed; network/name-resolution events are benign Azure agent and domain traffic
findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other and zeek there is no evidence of an adversary positioning in the middle of network traffic. The only network-configuration commands on the Windows hosts (arp.exe /a, route.exe print, netsh trace start/stop) were all spawned by legitimate Azure guest agents (WaAppAgent.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe, NetworkWatcherAgent.exe) on scranton.dmevals.local, i.e. routine Azure VM telemetry. DNS resolution (Sysmon 22) resolved only legitimate names to the domain controller 10.0.0.4 and Microsoft endpoints. SMB/RPC activity (5140/5145) was standard machine-account access to IPC$/SYSVOL (lsarpc/samr) between domain hosts. No relay, poisoning or interception tooling was found.

findings.title: No name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay; DNS and SMB activity is normal domain traffic
findings.summary: Sysmon DNS query events (event.code 22) on scranton/newyork/nashua resolved only legitimate names: the domain controller NEWYORK.dmevals.local -> 10.0.0.4, localhost, wec.dmevals.local -> 10.0.1.10, and Microsoft telemetry endpoints. No LLMNR/NBT-NS-style lookups or responses from unauthorized hosts were seen. The 4697/7045 service-install events were PsExec (PSEXESVC) and a 'Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service' (javamtsup.exe) — lateral movement/execution, not name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay. Zeek SMB activity (smb_mapping to \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\IPC$, kerberos cifs/NASHUA) is standard domain authentication. No relay tooling in PowerShell script blocks.

findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning; MAC anomalies are synthetic/placeholder values and arp.exe runs are Azure agent telemetry
findings.summary: Zeek conn records show source IP 10.0.1.4 with two different source MACs (00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and a responder MAC of 12:34:56:78:9a:bc. The 12:34:56:78:9a:bc address is a well-known synthetic/placeholder MAC used in Zeek test data, and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 is a locally-administered/randomized MAC — neither indicates a single attacker MAC claiming multiple IPs. The only ARP-related commands on the Windows hosts were 'arp.exe /a' invocations, all spawned by legitimate Azure guest agents (WaAppAgent.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe) on scranton.dmevals.local, i.e. routine Azure VM telemetry rather than attacker ARP reconnaissance.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing; no DHCP-related events or traffic observed
findings.summary: No DHCP spoofing indicators exist in the data. The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP-related event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063) — the stacked event codes are unrelated (5858/5857/7045/7040 etc.). Sysmon network-connect destination ports (event.code 3) show no DHCP traffic (no ports 67/68); the observed ports are normal (8443, 389, 88, 53, 135, 445, 443). The Zeek capture contains no dhcp log type (only conn/files/ssl/x509/dce_rpc/http/dns/kerberos/smb_*). The Dhcp client service (svchost -s Dhcp) start on scranton is a normal service start.

findings.title: Kerberos service-ticket requests for krbtgt and machine accounts by pbeesly (RC4)
findings.summary: On newyork.dmevals.local the account pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL requested Kerberos service tickets (event 4769) for machine accounts NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$ and notably for the krbtgt service (S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-502) with TicketOptions 0x60810010, all with TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (RC4). The repeated TGS requests for krbtgt and host SPNs from a single user, in the same window as the scranton credential-access activity, are consistent with Kerberoasting-style ticket harvesting, though no forged-ticket artifacts were observed.

findings.title: No golden-ticket indicators observed
findings.summary: No evidence of golden-ticket forging was found. All 28 Kerberos service-ticket requests (4769) used TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (RC4) with normal TicketOptions; there were no 4768/4769 anomalies, no krbtgt hash theft artifacts, and no PowerShell script blocks referencing golden/krbtgt (C312 zero hits). The krbtgt TGS requests seen are ordinary service-ticket requests, not forged TGTs.

findings.title: No silver-ticket indicators observed
findings.summary: No evidence of silver-ticket forging. The 4769 service-ticket requests for host SPNs (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) all carry normal TicketOptions and RC4 encryption and were issued by the KDC with Failure Code 0x0; no PowerShell script blocks referencing silver/service-ticket/SPN forging were found (C319 zero hits).

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting indicators observed
findings.summary: No evidence of AS-REP roasting. No PowerShell script blocks referencing AS-REP/asrep/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth were found (C334 zero hits), and no anomalous AS-REP request patterns were observed in the available data.

On scranton.dmevals.local (user pbeesly) a hidden, obfuscated PowerShell was launched from control.exe ("PowerShell.exe" -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden -c ... System.Drawing.Bitmap('C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png') ... IEX(...)), a steganographic loader. Shortly after, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1f3fff, consistent with credential material access. A later script block (Invoke-Exfil) compresses the Downloads folder with a password and copies it to a WebDAV share \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials. This is credential theft and exfiltration activity, but no artifact of forging web cookies or SAML tokens (T1606) was observed — the LSASS access is credential dumping, not web-credential forgery.

findings.title: No failed-logon or authentication-challenge burst in windows.security
findings.summary: Aggregating windows.security authentication events shows no 4625 (failed logon) events at all, and only a single 4776 credential-validation event (for pbeesly on newyork.dmevals.local). Successful logons (4624) are dominated by machine accounts (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$, UTICA$, WEC$) and SYSTEM, with pbeesly as the only interactive user. The 4648 explicit-credential events are routine (winlogon.exe for DWM/UMFD session accounts, taskhostw.exe, svchost.exe, and PSEXESVC.exe for pbeesly). This pattern is normal Windows authentication, not the repeated authentication-prompt flood characteristic of MFA request generation.

findings.title: PowerShell and Sysmon keyword hits are benign Windows components
findings.summary: The PowerShell 4104 hits matching 'authenticat' are a Microsoft module manifest (ModuleVersion 2.16.0.0, Author 'Microsoft Corporation') on newyork.dmevals.local, not MFA tooling. The Sysmon process-creation hits matching 'push' are the legitimate Windows services PushToInstall (svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s PushToInstall, started via sc.exe start pushtoinstall registration) and dmwappushservice on scranton.dmevals.local. Neither is an MFA push-notification generator. Zeek shows no MFA/identity-provider traffic (no okta/duo/mfa DNS queries or login/auth URLs); its 2140 events are conn/files/ssl/x509/dce_rpc/http/dns/kerberos/smb, with no authentication-prompt activity.

The only malicious artifact (Invoke-Exfil PowerShell using hardcoded creds for WebDAV exfil) is credential use/exfiltration, not MFA interception.
